Sections.Title: Overview
Sections.SubTitle: This year, over 100,000 developers told us how they learn, build their careers, which tools they’re using, and what they want in a job.

Sections.Title: Developer Profile
Sections.SubTitle: What we know about the developers who are writing the script for the future

Graphs.Title: Developer Type
Graphs.Copy: Over half of respondents identify as back-end developers, and about 20% work building mobile apps.

GraphCollections.Title: Contributing to Open Source
GraphCollections.Copy: Almost half of professional developers contribute to open source projects.

GraphCollections.Title: Coding as a Hobby
GraphCollections.Copy: Many developers work on code outside of work. Over 80% of our respondents say that they code as a hobby.

GraphCollections.Title: Years Since Learning to Code
GraphCollections.Copy: There is a wide range of experience levels among developers, and a full third of professional developers learned to code five years ago or less.

Graphs.Title: Years Coding Professionally
Graphs.Copy: Developers with many years of professional experience are rare.

GraphCollections.Title: Years of Professional Coding Experience by Developer Type

Graphs.Title: Years of Professional Coding Experience by Developer Type
Graphs.Copy: Developers who work in different areas of software development have different average amounts of experience. DevOps specialists and developers who code for desktop and enterprise applications have the most experience, while game/graphics developers and mobile developers have the fewest years of experience.

Graphs.Title: How Many Developers are Students?
Graphs.Copy: About one-quarter of respondents are enrolled in a formal college or university program full-time or part-time.

GraphCollections.Title: Educational Attainment
GraphCollections.Copy: Worldwide, about three-fourths of professional developers have the equivalent of a bachelor's degree or higher. It is not that rare to find accomplished professional developers who have not completed a degree.

GraphCollections.Title: Undergraduate Major
GraphCollections.Copy: Of professional developers who studied at the university level, over 60% said they majored in computer science, computer engineering, or software engineering. This proportion is somewhat higher in currently enrolled students, and the proportion of respondents majoring in other engineering disciplines like electrical and mechanical engineering is lower among current students than among professionals.

GraphCollections.Title: Other Types of Education
GraphCollections.Copy: Developers are lifelong learners; almost 90% of all developers say they have taught themselves a new language, framework, or tool outside of their formal education. Among professional developers, almost half say they have taken an online course like a MOOC, and about a quarter have participated in a hackathon.

GraphCollections.Title: Ways Developer Learn on Their Own
GraphCollections.Copy: Developers know how valuable good documentation is because they often use it when learning something new. Stack Overflow Q&A also ranks highly as a way to learn.

GraphCollections.Title: Why Do Developers Participate in Hackathons?

Graphs.Title: Why Do Developers Participate in Hackathons?
Graphs.Copy: We asked our respondents who said they have participated in hackathons or online coding competitions why they invest their time this way. The number one answer is that developers find these events enjoyable. These are also opportunities for learning, both general and specific.

Graphs.Title: Bootcamp Success
Graphs.Copy: Bootcamps are typically perceived as a way for newcomers to transition into a career as a software developer, but according to our survey, many participants in coding bootcamps were already working as developers. Almost half of our respondents who said they went to a coding bootcamp said they were already working as developers; these developers are likely updating their skills and moving to new areas of the tech industry. Of other bootcamp participants, the most common outcome is to find a job immediately or soon after graduating.

GraphCollections.Title: Gender
GraphCollections.Copy: We asked our respondents about their gender identity, and found that over 90% of our respondents are male. According to Quantcast, women account for about 10% of Stack Overflow’s US traffic; this year 9% of US survey respondents are women. We had survey participation at almost the rate we would expect from our traffic. In regions including the United States, India, and the UK, women are represented at higher levels among students than among professional developers.

GraphCollections.Title: Race and Ethnicity
GraphCollections.Copy: We see higher proportions of developers of color in students than professional developers. This year, 7.4% of professional developers in the United States identified as black, Hispanic or Latino/Latina, or Native American while over 10% of students in the United States identified as a member of one of these groups.

GraphCollections.Title: Sexual Orientation
GraphCollections.Copy: This is the first year we asked our respondents about their sexual orientation.

GraphCollections.Title: Parents' Education Level
GraphCollections.Copy: Like developers themselves, most developers' parents have the equivalent of a bachelor's degree or higher.

GraphCollections.Title: Disability Status
GraphCollections.Copy: We know developers can experience many forms of disability and difference, from mental health challenges to physical disability. Mental health issues like depression and anxiety are particularly common among our respondents.

Graphs.Title: Mental Health and Differences
Graphs.SubText: 11,431 responses identified as having a mental difference

Graphs.Title: Physical Differences
Graphs.SubText: 1,702 responses identified as having a physical difference

GraphCollections.Title: Age
GraphCollections.Copy: About three-fourths of professional developers who took our survey are younger than 35.

Graphs.Title: Developer Role and Gender
Graphs.Copy:
We find differences among developers by gender in our survey responses. For example, transgender and non-binary developers contribute to open source at higher rates (58% and 60%, respectively) than men or women (45% and 33%.)

We also see varying representation by men and women in different developer roles. All categories have dramatically more men than women but the ratio of men to women varies. Developers who are educators or academic researchers are about 10 times more likely to be men than women, while developers who are system admins or DevOps specialists are 25-30 times more likely to be men than women. Women have the highest representations as academics, QA developers, data scientists, and designers. These gender identifications are all 'select all that apply', so a developer can be counted in multiple categories.
Graphs.SubText: The dashed line shows the average ratio of men's to women's participation

GraphCollections.Title: Experience and Gender
GraphCollections.Copy: Twice as many women than men have been coding two years or less than men.

GraphCollections.Title: Age and Experience by Country
GraphCollections.Copy: Developers are older with more experience in countries in Western Europe and North America and younger with less experience in countries like India and Brazil.

Graphs.Title: Kinship, Competition, and Self-Evaluation
Graphs.Copy: We asked how much respondents agree or disagree with several statements about their place in the developer community. Overall 70% of developers agree or strongly agree that they feel a sense of connection with other developers. Developers are overall confident about their own skills compared to their peers, with only 18% agreeing or strongly agreeing that they are not as good at programming as their colleagues.
Graphs.SubText: 68,577 responses; agreement on a 1-5 scale, from strongly disagree to strongly agree

Graphs.Title: Experience and Belonging
Graphs.Copy: Developers' feelings on how much they belong and how they stack up to their peers change with how much experience they have. More experienced developers feel more connected, more confident, and less competitive. Notice that feeling less skilled drops quickly with experience while feeling less competitive drops more gradually and continues to drop into the second decade of coding experience.

Graphs.Title: Children and Other Dependents
Graphs.Copy: This year we asked respondents if they have children or other dependents that they care for, and about a quarter of respondents say that they do. We asked in a free response question what these developers do for dependent care during work hours, and our respondents talked about options like school, their spouses/partners, and daycare.

GraphCollections.Title: What Time Do Developers Wake Up?

Graphs.Title: What Time Do Developers Wake Up?
Graphs.Copy: We are confident that most developers have pulled a late night here and there, but most of our respondents say they are up by 8am.

GraphCollections.Title: How Much Time Do Developers Spend on a Computer?

Graphs.Title: How Much Time Do Developers Spend on a Computer?
Graphs.Copy: Our respondents include people who code as professionals, students, and hobbyists. The overwhelmingly majority spend large fractions of their waking hours on a typical day with their desktops and laptops.

GraphCollections.Title: How Much Time Do Developers Spend Outside?

Graphs.Title: How Much Time Do Developers Spend Outside?
Graphs.Copy: Developers get outside for recreation, commuting, or other reasons. About half of our respondents spend an hour or more outside a day.

GraphCollections.Title: Healthy Habits
GraphCollections.Copy: Developers tell us they do not often skip meals because of their workload, and a majority say they exercise at least some. The most often chosen exercise frequency is 'never', however.

Graphs.Title: How Often Do Developers Skip Meals To Be Productive?

GraphCollections.Title: Programming, Scripting, and Markup Languages
GraphCollections.Copy:
For the sixth year in a row, JavaScript is the most commonly used programming language. Python has risen in the ranks, surpassing C# this year, much like it surpassed PHP last year. Python has a solid claim to being the [fastest-growing major programming language](https://stackoverflow.blog/2017/09/06/incredible-growth-python/).

We see close alignment in the technology choices of professional developers and the developer population overall.

GraphCollections.Title: Frameworks, Libraries, and Tools
GraphCollections.Copy: Node.js and AngularJS continue to be the most commonly used technologies in this category, with React and .Net Core also important to many developers.

GraphCollections.Title: Databases
GraphCollections.Copy: Like last year, MySQL and SQL Server are the most commonly used databases.

GraphCollections.Title: Platforms
GraphCollections.Copy: Linux and Windows Desktop or Server are the most common choices that our respondents say they have done development work for this year.

GraphCollections.Title: Most Loved, Dreaded, and Wanted Languages
GraphCollections.Copy:
For the third year in a row, Rust is the most loved programming language among our respondents, followed close behind by Kotlin, a language we asked about for the first time on our survey this year. This means that proportionally, more developers want to continue working with these than other languages.

Also for the third year in a row, Visual Basic 6 ranks as the most dreaded programming language. Most dreaded means that a high percentage of developers who are currently using the technology express no interest in continuing to do so.

Python is the most wanted language for the second year in a row, meaning that it is the language that developers who do not yet use it most often say they want to learn.

Graphs.Title: Dreaded

Graphs.Title: Wanted

GraphCollections.Title: Most Loved, Dreaded, and Wanted Frameworks, Libraries, and Tools
GraphCollections.Copy: TensorFlow, one of the fastest growing technologies on Stack Overflow, is most loved by developers, while Cordova is most dreaded. React is the framework developers say they most want to work with if they do not already.

GraphCollections.Title: Most Loved, Dreaded, and Wanted Databases
GraphCollections.Copy: For the second year in a row, Redis is most loved database, meaning that proportionally more developers wanted to continue working with it than any other database. IMB's Db2 offering ranks as the most dreaded database, and for the second year in a row, MongoDB is the most wanted database.

GraphCollections.Title: Most Loved, Dreaded, and Wanted Platforms
GraphCollections.Copy: Linux is once again the most loved platform for development, with serverless infrastructure also loved this year. Sharepoint is the most dreaded development platform for the second year in a row, and many developers say they want to start developing for the Android platform and the Raspberry Pi.

GraphCollections.Title: Most Popular Development Environments
GraphCollections.Copy: Visual Studio Code just edged out Visual Studio as the most popular developer environment tool across the board, but there are differences in tool choices by developer type and role. Developers who write code for mobile apps are more likely to choose Android Studio and XCode, the most popular choice by DevOps and sysadmins is Vim, and data scientists are more likely to work in IPython/Jupyter, PyCharm, and RStudio.

GraphCollections.Title: Developers' Primary Operating Systems
GraphCollections.Copy: We asked our respondents what operating systems they use for work. About half said they mainly use Windows, and the remainder were about evenly split between MacOS and Linux.

Graphs.Title: How Many Monitors?
Graphs.Copy: The median number of monitors for respondents at their main workstation is two.

GraphCollections.Title: What Languages Are Associated with the Highest Salaries Worldwide?
GraphCollections.Copy: Globally, developers who use F#, Ocaml, Clojure, and Groovy earn the highest salaries, with median salaries above $70,000 USD. There are regional variations in which languages are associated with the highest pay. Erlang and Scala developers in the US are among the highest paid, while Clojure, Erlang, and Haskell developers earn the most in India.

Graphs.Title: How Technologies Are Connected
Graphs.Copy: Technologies cluster together into related ecosystems that tend to be used by the same developers. In this chart we a large central cluster for web development (with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS) connected via SQL to one for Microsoft technologies (with C#, Visual Studio, and .NET Core). Along the left we see a constellation connecting Java, Android, and iOS across to Linux, bash/shell, and Python. Other smaller correlated clusters include Scala/Spark, C/C++, and other smaller technologies that include language-specific IDEs.

GraphCollections.Title: What Do Developers Think Is Dangerous and Exciting About AI?
GraphCollections.Copy: Some types of developers are involved in the increasing role of machine learning and artificial intelligence in the world today, so we asked developers what they think is dangerous and exciting about these technologies. There is not much consensus among developers about what is most dangerous; each answer was chosen roughly equally. The top choice for what is exciting about increasing AI is that jobs can be automated.

GraphCollections.Title: Who is Primary Responsible for Considering the Ramifications of AI?

Graphs.Title: Who is Primary Responsible for Considering the Ramifications of AI?
Graphs.Copy: Developers are most likely to think that the creators and technologists behind the machine learning and AI algorithms are the ones who are ultimately most responsible for the societal issues surrounding artificial intelligence. About a quarter of respondents think that a regulatory body should be primarily responsible.

GraphCollections.Title: How Do Developers Feel About the Future of AI?

Graphs.Title: How Do Developers Feel About the Future of AI?
Graphs.Copy: Developers are mostly optimistic about the possibilities that artificial intelligence offers our world, with almost three-fourths of respondents saying that they are overall more excited than worried about the AI future.

Graphs.Title: AI Concerns by Developer Type
Graphs.Copy: The concerns that developers bring to issues around artificial intelligence depend on the kind of coding work they do. For example, data scientists are 1.5 times more likely to consider issues around algorithmic fairness dangerous than any upcoming singularity, the most of any kind of developer. We included a free response option on this question; there was not much serious worry about Skynet, but many developers discussed systemic bias being built into algorithmic decision making and the danger of AI being used without the ability to inspect and reason about decision pathways.

Sections.Title: Work
Sections.SubTitle: How developers get down to the business of software

GraphCollections.Title: Employment Status
GraphCollections.Copy: Over three-fourths of professional developers are employed full time, and 10% work as independent contractors, freelancers, or are self-employed.

GraphCollections.Title: Employment Status by Geography
GraphCollections.Copy: Germany has an unusually high proportion of developers working part-time, and developers in the United States are somewhat less likely to work as independent contractors or freelancers.

GraphCollections.Title: Employment Status for Professional Developers by Geography
GraphCollections.Copy: Respondents who are professional developers are employed full-time at higher rates than respondents in general.

GraphCollections.Title: Industry
GraphCollections.Copy: Software developers work in a diverse range of industries (so diverse that it's hard to ask about them all in one question!) both inside and outside the technology industry. Our answer choices focused on the tech industry this year, and of these choices, more professional developers work for companies doing web development, IT, and SaaS.

Graphs.Title: Company Size
Graphs.Copy: Developers work in companies of all sizes, from quite small to large enterprise organizations. More software developers in the United States work at larger companies compared to the rest of the world.

GraphCollections.Title: What Do Developers Hope To Be Doing in Five Years?
GraphCollections.Copy: Developers' career goals are largely focused on technical work, with just over half of respondents saying they want to be in the same or a different technical role in the future. About a quarter of developers say they want to create their own company.

GraphCollections.Title: How Do Developers Feel About Their Careers and Jobs?
GraphCollections.Copy: Developers tend to be satisfied with their career, more so in general than with their current job. Overall, career satisfaction does not vary significantly by industry. However, current job satisfaction is significantly lower for developers working in financial services and IT.

GraphCollections.Title: What Would Developers Do If Asked to Write Code for an Unethical Purpose?

Graphs.Title: What Would Developers Do If Asked to Write Code for an Unethical Purpose?
Graphs.Copy: When posed with a hypothetical situation where they are asked to write code for a product or purpose that they consider clearly unethical, over half of our respondents say that they would not write such code. Ethical situations can be complicated, and about another third say that it would depend on the situation.

GraphCollections.Title: How Would Developers Report Ethical Problems with Code?

Graphs.Title: How Would Developers Report Ethical Problems with Code?
Graphs.Copy: The question of what to do *next* after an ethical problem has arisen is even more tricky, according to our respondents. The most common answer, from almost half of respondents, is that how to report an ethical problem depends on the particulars of any given situation.

GraphCollections.Title: Who Is Ultimately Most Responsible for Code That Accomplishes Something Unethical?

Graphs.Title: Who Is Ultimately Most Responsible for Code That Accomplishes Something Unethical?
Graphs.Copy: Most developers feel that management is ultimately most accountable for unethical results of code; a developer who writes code used for unethical purposes was the least likely choice on this question.

GraphCollections.Title: Do Developers Have an Obligation to Consider the Ethical Implications of Their Code?

Graphs.Title: Do Developers Have an Obligation to Consider the Ethical Implications of Their Code?
Graphs.Copy: Almost 80% of respondents affirm that considering what their code can be used for is the right thing for developers to do. We included a free response opportunity after this question, and we saw thoughtful reflections from developers. These include responses about how the tools developers build are powerful and come with a lot of responsibility, situations where unethical outcomes may accidentally arise, and how large teams are involved in building software but developers can be the last line of defense against unethical code.

Graphs.Title: Job Search Status
Graphs.Copy: Only 16% of developers are actively looking for a job, but about three-fourths of developers are interested in hearing about new job opportunities.

GraphCollections.Title: Job Search Status by Geography
GraphCollections.Copy: Job seeking status is largely consistent across the US, UK, Germany, and Canada.

GraphCollections.Title: Who's Actively Looking for a Job?

Graphs.Title: Who's Actively Looking for a Job?
Graphs.Copy: Among professional developers, those who work at the C-level and as engineering managers or product managers are looking for work the least. Mobile developers and game/graphics developers are actively looking for work at higher proportions

GraphCollections.Title: How Long Ago Did Developers Last Change Jobs?

Graphs.Title: How Long Ago Did Developers Last Change Jobs?
Graphs.Copy: About half of developers have taken a new job within the past two years; frequent job changes are the norm for software developers.

GraphCollections.Title: Job Change Timelines by Geography
GraphCollections.Copy: Across the US, UK, Germany, and Canada, software developers change jobs at about the same rates.

GraphCollections.Title: Developer Opinions About Searching for Job
GraphCollections.Copy: We asked developers what they found annoying, exhausting, interesting, and exciting about the process of searching for a new job in separate free response questions. Respondents talked about the new opportunities, technologies, and people that a new job can offer, but expressed frustration with broken processes around interviews and recruiting.

GraphCollections.Title: How Do Developers Assess Potential Jobs?

Graphs.Title: How Do Developers Assess Potential Jobs?
Graphs.Copy: In general, developers' top priority in assessing a job is compensation, followed by the specific technologies that they will work with.
Graphs.SubText: 66,985 responses; average ranking in order of importance

GraphCollections.Title: Differences in Assessing Jobs by Gender
GraphCollections.Copy: Different types of developers apply different sets of priorities when considering jobs. Developers who are not men rank the company culture and office environment as their highest concern when assessing a new job.

Graphs.Title: Men
Graphs.SubText: 54,536 responses; average ranking in order of importance

Graphs.SubText: 4,026 responses; average ranking in order of importance

Graphs.SubText: 813 responses; average ranking in order of importance

GraphCollections.Title: What Developers Value in Compensation and Benefits

Graphs.Title: What Developers Value in Compensation and Benefits
Graphs.Copy: Developers prioritize salary highest, with other considerations like computer equipment and conference budgets ranking lower.
Graphs.SubText: 64,918 responses; average ranking in order of importance

GraphCollections.Title: Valuing Compensation and Benefits by Geography
GraphCollections.Copy: The specifics of how developers are compensated with salary and benefits work differently across the world, so developer responses vary by geography. Health insurance is prioritized in countries without a national healthcare system (like the United States), and pension benefits are unusually important to developers in the UK.

GraphCollections.Title: What Do Developers Use to Stay Comfortable While Working?

Graphs.Title: What Do Developers Use to Stay Comfortable While Working?
Graphs.Copy: Standing desks are not confined to trendy Silicon Valley offices; over half of our respondents say they use one, almost the same proportion who use a device like an ergonomic keyboard or mouse.

GraphCollections.Title: Which Methodologies Do Developers Use?
GraphCollections.Copy: Agile and Scrum are popular methodologies for developers to keep their projects on track.

GraphCollections.Title: How Long Do Developers Expect New Coworkers to Take to Be Productive?

Graphs.Title: How Long Do Developers Expect New Coworkers to Take to Be Productive?
Graphs.Copy: We asked our respondents to imagine they had a new coworker with four years of relevant experience joining their team, and then to estimate how long that person would take to become fully productive and contribute at a typical level. About three-fourths of developers thought that hypothetical new coworker would be fully up to speed within three months or less.

GraphCollections.Title: Version Control
GraphCollections.Copy: Git is the dominant choice for version control for developers today, with almost 90% of developers checking in their code via git.

GraphCollections.Title: How Often Do Developers Check In Code?
GraphCollections.Copy: The majority of developers check in code multiple times per day, and professional developers are less likely to check in code never or rarely.

GraphCollections.Title: How are Job Satisfaction and Committing Code Related?

Graphs.Title: How are Job Satisfaction and Committing Code Related?
Graphs.Copy: Developers who check in code the most often also have higher job satisfaction.
Graphs.SubText: Mean of 59,260 responses; satisfaction on a 1-7 scale, from extremely dissatisfied to extremely satisfied

GraphCollections.Title: Salary by Developer Type
GraphCollections.Copy:
Engineering managers, DevOps specialists, and data scientists command the highest salaries. See our [Methodology](https://insights.stackoverflow.com/survey/2018#methodology) section for information on how we converted local currencies used by respondents to U.S. dollars.

Average top earners vary by geography. In India, for example, data scientists are among the top earners, while in European countries, back-end developers and developers working with embedded devices are among the top earners.

GraphCollections.Title: Salary and Experience by Developer Type

Graphs.Title: Salary and Experience by Developer Type
Graphs.Copy: Developers with more years of experience are paid more, naturally, but we also see that some type of coding work is paid more highly at the same level of experience. Data scientists and DevOps specialists are high earners for their level of experience.

Graphs.Title: Salary and Experience by Language
Graphs.Copy: Developers using languages that appear above the blue line in this chart such as Go, Clojure, and F# are being paid more even given how much experience they have. Developers using languages below the blue line like PHP and Visual Basic 6, however, are paid less even given years of experience. The size of the circles in this chart represents how many developers are using that language compared to the others.

Sections.Title: Community
Sections.SubTitle: Where developers come to learn, share knowledge, and build their careers

Graphs.Title: Visiting Stack Overflow
Graphs.Copy: Developers visit Stack Overflow. A lot. Stack Overflow is the largest, most trusted online developer community and over half of our respondents say they are at least daily visitors. Our users also feel very positively about Stack Overflow. We asked a traditional [net promoter score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Net_Promoter) question for Stack Overflow as a whole and our NPS is 75, a world class score according to benchmarks.

GraphCollections.Title: How Many Participants Have a Stack Overflow Account?

Graphs.Title: How Many Participants Have a Stack Overflow Account?
Graphs.Copy: Almost 90% of the participants in our survey are registered users with accounts.

GraphCollections.Title: Sharing What You've Built in Your Developer Story

Graphs.Title: Sharing What You've Built in Your Developer Story
Graphs.Copy: Only 17% of respondents have an up-to-date Developer Story here on Stack Overflow. You can [create your own Developer Story](https://stackoverflow.com/users/story/join) to show what matters most to you as a developer.

GraphCollections.Title: How Often Do Developers Participate on Stack Overflow?

Graphs.Title: How Often Do Developers Participate on Stack Overflow?
Graphs.Copy: Some developers come to Stack Overflow only to find answers to their questions, and some participate in the community by asking, answering, voting for, or commenting on questions. The most common participation frequency in our survey participants is about monthly.

GraphCollections.Title: How Do Do Developers Feel About Ads?

Graphs.Title: How Do Do Developers Feel About Ads?
Graphs.Copy: Like many websites, Stack Overflow has ads, and we want to know how to make our ads more relevant for our users. Over half of our respondents agreed or strongly agreed that they enjoy seeing online updates from companies they like and that online advertising can be valuable when it is relevant. A full 40% of developers say they fundamentally dislike the concept of advertising.
Graphs.SubText: 74,710 responses; agreement on a 1-5 scale, from strongly disagree to strongly agree

Graphs.Title: Ad Priorities for Developers
Graphs.Copy: In general, developers' top priority in assessing an advertisement is whether it is relevant to them, followed by whether it provides useful information and is trustworthy. Developers are not swayed by free offers in advertisements.
Graphs.SubText: 60,479 responses; average ranking in order of importance

GraphCollections.Title: Do Developers Consider Themselves Part of the Stack Overflow Community?
GraphCollections.Copy: Most of the respondents to our survey consider themselves part of our community, but this varies for different groups of people. For example, we find that respondents who identify as male see themselves as part of the community at higher rates than those with other gender identities. The tech community as a whole and we as Stack Overflow in particular still have work to do in this area.

Graphs.Title: Percent Who Consider Themselves Part of the Stack Overflow Community by Gender
Graphs.SubText: Mean of 64,804 responses; gender is select all that apply

GraphCollections.Title: Interest in Hypothetical New Tools on Stack Overflow

Graphs.Title: Interest in Hypothetical New Tools on Stack Overflow
Graphs.Copy: As we work to make our community a better place for developers to learn, share, and grow their careers, we asked our survey respondents about their interest in possible new tools. An employer review system and help with career growth garnered the most interest.
Graphs.SubText: 70,687 responses; interest on a 1-5 scale, from not at all interested to extremely interested

GraphCollections.Title: What Words Do Developers Use to Describe Stack Overflow?
GraphCollections.Copy: In these free response questions, we asked developers first to describe the Stack Overflow community in general, and then what they would change about it. Developers were largely positive about Stack Overflow, focusing on the helpful nature of the community, and specifically had ideas about how questions, answers, comments, and reputation are handled. The treatment of new users and new people in our community were mentioned often as well.

Graphs.Title: Top 20 Words Used to Describe the Stack Overflow Community
Graphs.SubText: 5,209 responses; % of respondents who used each word

Graphs.Title: Top 20 Words Used to Suggest Changes to Stack Overflow
Graphs.SubText: 3,453 responses; % of respondents who used each word

Graphs.Title: Developers' Perspectives About Our Community
Graphs.Copy: Our survey this year included questions about what developers think the best, worst, most annoying, and most exciting things about Stack Overflow are. (These questions were randomized so that each respondent got one positive and one negative version.) In the positive versions of these questions, respondents were more likely to talk about the wealth of sharing and collaboration on our site. In the negative versions, respondents reflected on harsh interactions they've witnessed, downvotes, and handling of duplicate questions.

Sections.Title: Methodology
Sections.SubTitle: How we planned and analyzed our survey
